This page explains, in general terms and without code, the data a study like this one rests on: what the United States Renal Data System and the Medical Evidence form are, how kidney function at the start of dialysis is estimated, how a patient is placed in a health care area, and where area-level information comes from. How such data are analysed is on [Statistical methods](statistical_methods.qmd); what this study chose is on [Study design and methods](study_methods.qmd).

## The United States Renal Data System

The United States Renal Data System (USRDS) is a national data system on chronic kidney disease and kidney failure in the United States, funded by the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases [@usrds2024guide]. Researchers receive it as a set of files linked by one patient identifier. Two matter most for studying how dialysis begins:

-   the **Medical Evidence file**, which holds the forms completed when a person starts treatment for kidney failure;
-   the **Residence file**, which holds a person's residential ZIP code and state as a series of periods with start and end dates [@usrds2024guide].

The meaning of each coded value is given by a named list of codes (a *format*) in the USRDS Researcher's Guide [@usrds2024guide]. Formats can change between releases, so code written for one release needs checking against the formats of the release it runs on.

## The Medical Evidence form

The CMS-2728 End Stage Renal Disease Medical Evidence Report is completed when a person starts regular dialysis or receives a kidney transplant, including a transplant instead of a course of dialysis [@cms2728_form; @cms2728_form2015; @usrds2024guide]. It records, at that moment, demographics (age, sex, race, Hispanic ethnicity); coexisting conditions as yes/no fields; laboratory values before the first dialysis, including creatinine, albumin and hemoglobin; the type and setting of dialysis, the vascular access and insurance; whether the patient saw a nephrologist beforehand; and the primary cause of kidney failure, as a code from a list CMS publishes [@cms2728_causes].

Coexisting conditions are those the facility recorded, not confirmed by separate review. When checked against clinical records, the form's conditions were often missing where present (average sensitivity 0.59) but rarely recorded where absent (specificity above 0.95) [@longenecker2000validation]. A person can have more than one form, for example after recovering kidney function and later restarting dialysis, so studies of the first start use the earliest.

## Estimated GFR at the start of dialysis

The glomerular filtration rate (GFR) measures how much blood the kidneys filter each minute. It is rarely measured directly; in practice it is *estimated* (eGFR) from serum creatinine with an equation, in mL/min/1.73 m² (adjusted to a standard body size) [@stevens2006gfr]. Creatinine results depend on the laboratory method; standardizing them across laboratories was recommended in 2006 [@myers2006creatinine]. The CKD-EPI equation published in 2009 uses creatinine, age, sex and race, and gives a higher eGFR to a patient recorded as Black than to another with the same creatinine [@levey2009ckdepi]. Equations published in 2021 leave race out [@inker2021ckdepi], and US nephrology societies recommend them [@delgado2022unifying].

The eGFR at the start of dialysis describes *when* in the course of kidney disease dialysis began; a start at a higher eGFR is often called an **early start**. The IDEAL trial randomized adults to start dialysis at a higher or a lower estimated GFR and found no survival benefit from starting earlier [@cooper2010ideal]; IDEAL estimated GFR with the Cockcroft-Gault equation, not CKD-EPI, so its thresholds do not carry over exactly to CKD-EPI values. Studies have asked what, besides the patient's kidney function, influences when dialysis starts, including how much it varies between areas and how local care is organized [@ohare2010regional; @scialla2014iv; @li2017trends; @hemmige2024density]. Most of that variation remains unexplained by recorded patient and physician characteristics [@li2017trends]. The form records a creatinine value from the 45 days before the first dialysis [@cms2728_form2015], so the eGFR at initiation approximates, rather than records, the value clinicians saw when they decided to start.

## Dialysis facility listings

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) publishes lists of dialysis facilities, with each facility's ZIP code, stations and ownership, and archives earlier releases [@cms2025dfc]. Each release describes the facilities at that time, so the facilities near a patient on a given date come from the release current on that date.

## Hospital Service Areas

The Dartmouth Atlas of Health Care divides the United States into Hospital Service Areas (HSAs): groups of ZIP codes whose residents receive most of their hospital care locally [@dartmouth_faq]. Each ZIP code is assigned to the area where the largest share of its residents' hospital stays took place, which need not be a majority [@dartmouth_methods]. An HSA is a local health care market rather than a political boundary. The Atlas publishes a crosswalk assigning each ZIP code to an HSA for each year, because ZIP codes are added and retired [@dartmouth_crosswalks].

The Atlas also publishes measures for each HSA, such as the share of Medicare enrollees with diabetes who receive eye examinations and HbA1c testing, the rate of hospital discharges for conditions that good outpatient care can often prevent (ambulatory-sensitive discharges), and hospital beds and staff per resident [@dartmouth_primarycare; @dartmouth_capacity]. Beds and staff are allocated to HSAs by where each hospital's Medicare patients live, not by where the hospital stands, and are expressed per resident of all ages [@dartmouth_methods]. Values too small to be reliable, and values suppressed, are stored as special negative codes; these are flags, not numbers, and are treated as missing [@dartmouth_primarycare].

## ZIP codes and ZCTAs

ZIP codes are mail delivery routes, not areas with fixed boundaries, and they are added, changed and retired [@grubesic2006zcta]. The Census Bureau publishes its statistics for ZIP Code Tabulation Areas (ZCTAs), areas built to approximate the territory of ZIP codes [@census_zcta]. Most ZIP codes have a ZCTA with the same number, but not every ZIP code has one [@census_zcta]; a ZIP code with no territory of its own, such as one used only for post office boxes, is counted within a surrounding ZCTA [@grubesic2006zcta].

Linking a ZIP code to Census data therefore needs a crosswalk from ZIP code to ZCTA. The UDS Mapper published one for each year, and the [{zippeR}](https://github.com/pfizer-opensource/zippeR) R package makes them available [@uds_crosswalk; @zipper_pkg]. Matching by number alone loses the people living in ZIP codes whose ZCTA has a different number.

## American Community Survey estimates

The American Community Survey (ACS) is a continuous survey run by the Census Bureau. For small areas such as ZCTAs it publishes *5-year estimates*, which pool 60 months of responses; an estimate labelled with a year describes the five years ending in that year, not that year alone [@census2020acshandbook]. A *subject table* gathers many characteristics of an area (population, race, income, poverty) in one place [@census2020acshandbook]. The [{tidycensus}](https://walker-data.com/tidycensus/) R package downloads ACS tables [@tidycensus]. The Census Bureau changes tables between releases [@census_acs_tablechanges], so the codes that identify variables can change, and each year's labels need checking.

## Rural-urban commuting area codes

The US Department of Agriculture's Economic Research Service publishes Rural-Urban Commuting Area (RUCA) codes, which classify areas by population density, urbanization and daily commuting [@ers2020ruca]. Its ZIP code file gives each ZIP code a primary code, from metropolitan core to rural, with a separate code for ZIP codes with no population. The primary codes are commonly grouped into metropolitan, micropolitan, small town and rural areas [@ers2020ruca; @ers_ruca_documentation].
